# v1.2.12 — CGBUM chapters actually load

## The bug

Opening any CGBUM chapter showed blank pages. The images never arrived, so the
reader sat on placeholders no matter how long you waited.

The cause was not, as an earlier note claimed, that the image host blocks
datacenter traffic. The real reason is that CGBUM's chapter image server
(`cdn8.cgbum.com`) refuses every request that does not carry a special
`cgbum_reader_ts` cookie, which the chapter page itself hands out when it
loads. That cookie is marked HttpOnly, so the app's WebView cannot read it, and
it also expects a `cgbum.com` referer. The backend captured neither, so every
image came back rejected and the reader had nothing to show.

## The fix

- **The backend now keeps the cookie.** When it fetches a chapter page it reads
  the cookie the page sets and attaches it to each image in that chapter.
- **The image proxy forwards it — but only where it belongs.** The cookie is
  passed on only for CGBUM's own hosts, so the proxy cannot be used to leak
  cookies to arbitrary sites.
- **Offline downloads send it too.** Downloading a chapter for offline reading
  now presents the same cookie and referer, so saved chapters actually contain
  images instead of error pages.
- **Covers were never affected** and still load as before.

The result: CGBUM chapter pages load normally, in the reader and in downloads.

## Notes

- The earlier v1.2.9 note blaming datacenter IP blocking has been corrected. The
  host was reachable all along; it was waiting for the cookie.

# v1.2.11 — Updates you can actually trust

## The old updater never worked, and it was dangerous

Two problems sat underneath the update system, and neither was visible from
the outside.

The first was that updates silently did nothing. The app shipped with Capgo's
Capacitor updater enabled, but the WebView is pointed at the embedded Node
server on `http://localhost:3000`, not at the Capgo-managed bundle folder. So
Capgo could download and "activate" a new web bundle all day long and the app
would keep serving the old files from disk. Every update looked successful and
changed nothing.

The second was worse. The Node backend exposed `/api/internal/update`, which
accepted a bundle from any caller on the machine and wrote it straight into
the running app. No signature, no hash, no authentication. Anything that could
reach that port could replace the code the app runs.

Both are gone. Updates now flow through a single signed channel, and the old
unsigned endpoints have been removed entirely.

## How updates work now

- **Signed releases.** Every update is described by a manifest that lists the
  version, the download URL, the file size, and a SHA-256 hash of the bundle.
  The manifest is signed in CI with an Ed25519 key. The app carries only the
  public key and refuses anything whose signature does not verify.
- **Verified before install.** The app downloads the bundle, checks its size
  and SHA-256 against the signed manifest, rejects any archive entry that
  escapes the target directory, then installs it atomically. A bundle that
  fails any check never touches the running app.
- **Safe boots with rollback.** A new bundle gets three chances to start. If
  it throws or the app cannot confirm a clean boot, the app falls back to the
  previous version automatically. Only the three most recent bundles are kept
  on disk.
- **Honest version gates.** The feed records a minimum app version, so an
  update that needs a newer native shell is skipped rather than installed and
  broken. Downgrades and versions you have already rolled back are refused.
- **No restart guesswork.** Applying an update restarts the embedded runtime
  cleanly instead of relying on the activity to be recreated, which fixes the
  old "launch it twice" behavior.

## In the app

Account → Updates now reflects reality:

- **Check for updates** asks the signed feed, not a dead backend.
- **Install** appears only when a verified update is waiting, and shows the
  release notes for that version before you tap it.
- **Release notes** are fetched from the same feed, so the changelog you read
  matches the build that was published.

## For maintainers

- A single command publishes a release: it builds the web bundle and backend,
  zips the payload, signs the manifest, opens the GitHub release, and refreshes
  the feed. A preflight check refuses to publish unless the version matches in
  `package.json`, `app.js`, the Gradle build, and a non-empty changelog.
- The private signing key lives only in CI secrets and a local `.secrets/`
  file that is git-ignored. It is never committed.
- The publish job runs the full test suite first and stops if anything fails.

## Notes

- The legacy `backend-update.js` payload and its boot path have been removed;
  an installed copy is cleaned up on first launch.
- If you build the app yourself, run `npm run ota:keys` once to generate a
  keypair, then put the printed public key into the manifest module and keep
  the private key out of version control.
